chapter: Leading the band after Chick Webb, 1939-40
title: Ella hands over the baton; Elmer Williams rejoins
summary: In Chicago, Ella told McRae to lead the band, Babe Wallace had disappeared, and Elmer Williams borrowed a tenor from Coleman Hawkins.

bands.name: Ella Fitzgerald and Her Famous Orchestra

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Playing in Lionel Hampton's big band

blocks.x: We went to Pittsburgh and (inaudible) through the middle west and (inaudible). We was on our way to (inaudible). We were working -- we were doing one nighters heading into Chicago (inaudible). We played a theater out there. Colored

theater in Chicago like the Apollo Theater. I forget the name of that theater on the south side. You know, a very famous theater.
It's like the Apollo Theater here. I'll think of it later.
Well now, we're on our way to play the Chicago theater. It's not the Chicago theater -- colored theater on the West side. (inaudible).

And the night before -- the night we was playing the one nighters before we go in Chicago, Ella Fitzgerald come to me about twelve o'clock. Said, "I can't make it anymore (inaudible). You have to lead the band."
Remember, Ella was conducting the band all the time. She was standing out in front waving her hand, you know.
And it was just too much for her -- to stand up there and sing all those numbers and then, you know, conducting the band, you know.
She come to me -- she said, "Teddy, I just can't make it anymore. I'm going to give it to you because you got it. You got it tomorrow in the

theater."
I said, "Okay."
Now --
Bardu Ali in presence was missed
No. Bardu --
He wasn't there, but his presence was missed, I'm sure.

Yeah. Bardu Ali had left us before we went on the tour. We had Babe Wallace. Remember I told you we got Babe Wallace to stand for... (inaudible)? But somehow, when we got to Pittsburgh, we were playing a -- we were playing Pittsburgh on this particular date.
When we got ready to leave Pittsburgh, we couldn't find Babe Wallace. We looked all over, sent back to the hotel, and he was, like, disappeared or something. Like he didn't want to go any further with the band.
Because he was in front of the band. He looked good, he was doing a great job. Sing good and everything.
But it was just something missing with

him, you know. Just something -- he was doing good but it was just something that wasn't there, you know.
So he decided he didn't want to go -- I guess in his mind. Well, we're going to leave so we left. On our way to the Midwest, (inaudible) to that way Cleveland, Ohio (inaudible).
So, Ella was conducting the band -- was out front there. It was just too much for her.
So when we got to -- the night before we went to Chicago, she said, "Well you have to take over the band."
Now I'm (inaudible) sitting down playing. I haven't (inaudible) the band (inaudible) I know everything.
I know all about the arrangements, so I said okay.
So now, I get to Chicago -- I got a couple of days before I go into the theater -- Elmer Williams who used to be with the band -- the tenor player used to be with Chick -- he was in Chicago.
He had been in Chicago. He moved out to

Chicago -- working around Chicago.
So, at that time he wasn't working. And
when I got in town, I looked Elmer up -- I say, "Look,
what are you doing? I need a tenor player. Why
don't you come on and go to the coast with us?"
"We're going to California, you
always wanted to go to California. We're going out
to play in California. We you come back -- if you
don't want to go back to New York, you can leave us
here, because we're coming back here to play the
Savoy Ballroom"
He says, "Okay."
So now, Elmer don't have a horn. We
got to look all over New York to get a horn. Elmer
say, "Coleman Hawkins is in town. I think I can
borrow one of Coleman's tenors."
So, Coleman lent him the tenor -- you
know, by knowing the band and Ella and everything,
Coleman let Elmer have one of his tenors.
Coleman always had a couple of tenors
(Inaudible), you know. He'd carry one or two with him
all the time in case something happen to one.
So he let Elmer have one of his tenors.
And Elmer played the whole week in the theater with us there, and I conducted the band, that was the first week. (inaudible).
By the end of the week, I had got used to it.
So you were --
Oh yeah, I was (inaudible).
Stand in front of the band and --
The second day I was in front of the band and playing and everything. I was, you know,-- wasn't no sweating, you know. I was really...
Were you still a featured tenor soloist?
Oh yeah. Everything. Announcer and everything. I was really with it then. After the second day, forget it. I was on my way, you know.
Now we get to California --
Now we're going to the theater in California --
